claims.explanation: Chlorambucil is a bifunctional alkylating agent whose cytotoxicity depends on DNA adduct formation and mismatch-repair-driven futile cycling, so selectivity is best explained by loss of DNA-damage/apoptosis effectors and by detoxification or repair pathways. The most consistent genomic pattern in sensitive lines is combined TP53 pathway disruption with intact alkylation-damage processing, whereas resistant lines tend to retain TP53 or have lesions that blunt alkylator-induced death (e.g., ATM loss, KEAP1/NFE2L2 activation, metallothionein-mediated detoxification). Features such as KEAP1/NFE2L2 mutation, metallothionein overexpression, and MMR loss are mechanistically supported by the retrieved abstracts and predict resistance rather than sensitivity.

features.basis: TP53-mutant lines dominate the sensitive set and TP53 loss impairs DNA-damage-induced apoptosis after alkylation
KEAP1 loss activates NRF2 and is associated with alkylator/chemoresistance in the retrieved NRF2 regulation abstract
NFE2L2 activation drives antioxidant programs that detoxify alkylating agents
Metallothionein overexpression confers cross-resistance to chlorambucil and melphalan
ATM loss blunts DNA-damage signaling and is enriched in the least-affected lines
High MCL1 correlates with failure to achieve remission after chlorambucil
BCL2-family anti-apoptotic proteins limit alkylator-induced apoptosis in CLL
MMR loss prevents futile repair cycling and cytotoxic DSBs from alkylation damage
MMR deficiency causes resistance to alkylating-agent cytotoxicity
MGMT directly repairs O6-alkylguanine adducts and limits alkylator toxicity
PTEN loss is frequent in sensitive lines and may impair survival signaling after DNA damage
BRAF-mutant melanoma and other lines are enriched among sensitive lines, possibly reflecting MAPK-driven apoptotic priming
